To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the FDR is an appropriate approach in disease mapping and in descriptive epidemiology.

1) FDR procedures are adequate to screen for areas or diseases with altered risk; 2) FDR procedures provide more power than the Bonferrioni correction for multiple testing; 3) The q-value, the FDR analogue to the p-value, can be used to assess the statistical significance of the results of disease mapping studies.
the FDR is a useful tool to control the multiplicity problem and that it is more powerful than the Bonferrioni correction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of statistical methods for disease mapping.
the development of statistical methodology for the analysis of spatial data.
the problem of multiple testing and the control of FWER in the context of disease mapping and descriptive studies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FDR procedures should be used in disease mapping to screen for areas with altered risk.
the FDR procedure is an adequate tool to screen for areas or diseases at high/low risk, and it is a useful procedure as complementary to point estimates and to the confidence intervals.
the FDR procedure is a useful tool for screening for disease excess/ deficit and high/low risk regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in disease mapping, the FDR approach should be considered as an alternative to the Bonferrioni correction.
the use of FDR in disease mapping and epidemiological descriptive studies is a valid and useful procedure to control the false discovery rate.
FDR is a useful tool for the detection of high/low risk regions in disease mapping.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of unadjusted p-values to identify multiple areas or diseases with altered risk is inappropriate.
the FDR is a powerful tool for the analysis of multiple testing in disease mapping.
the FDR procedure should be considered in disease mapping and other descriptive epidemiological studies where the number of hypotheses is large.
